title: Icon sets that stay quiet
excerpt: Use one stroke, one grid, and one weight for the icons on a site. Mixed styles in a single header make the page look assembled from downloads.
alt: Hands sketching a user-flow diagram labeled user goals on a sheet of paper. The drawn diagram fits a piece about icons that should follow one quiet system.
caption: One stroke, drawn on purpose, is enough. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: How many icon styles should a website use?
faqs.answer: One. Same stroke width, same grid, same corner style, and the same visual weight, so mixed drawings do not make the header look collected from different libraries. If a single icon needs to be bolder, redraw it inside the system. Do not import a second family for one moment.

faqs.question: Do icons need text labels?
faqs.answer: When the meaning is not already obvious and repeated, yes. A menu mark and a close mark are widely understood, and they still need an accessible name in the markup, while a custom metaphor needs a visible word. The W3C's WCAG principles call for controls a person can operate and understand. A silent picture fails that.

faqs.question: Where should the icon set live?
faqs.answer: In the same system as the type and the color, with the source files and a short note about stroke and grid. Engineers should be able to use a named icon without redrawing it. When the stroke changes, it changes once. A folder of loose SVGs on someone's desktop will drift the first week someone is in a hurry.

markdown:
Pick one stroke, one grid, and one weight, and use them everywhere. That is a quiet icon style for websites. Three styles in one header, an outline mark next to a filled mark next to something from a different decade of the internet, make the site look assembled from downloads. The visitor may not name the problem. They will feel that the page was not finished by the same hands.

Icons are support. They help a person spot Search, Close, or a short list of features. They are not the brand voice. The word does that job. When the icon gets louder than the word, the page is decorated instead of directed.

## One stroke, one grid, one weight

Choose a stroke and keep it. A 1.5 pixel line and a 3 pixel line in the same navigation do not look like a choice. They look like two files. Corners should agree too. Round caps on one icon and sharp corners on the next are a second split. Pick the family that matches the type: a geometric wordmark can take a geometric icon, a softer wordmark can take a softer terminal. Then stop varying it.

Draw on a grid. A 24-pixel grid is a common working size for interface icons, with the artwork sitting slightly inside the box so optical edges line up. The grid is there so a plus sign and an arrow feel like the same weight when they sit in a row. Without it, someone nudges each icon until the row looks accidentally even, and the next person undoes it.

Weight means how much ink is in the box. Outlined icons in a row, or filled icons in a row. Mixing them to mean "active" can work if the filled version is the same drawing with the interior painted, not a different metaphor. Active, hover, and disabled are states of one icon. They are not invitations to a new style.

Color stays quiet too. Icons inherit the text color beside them, or a single muted color you already use for secondary text. A rainbow row of feature icons is a poster. It pulls the eye off the sentence under each one. If color carries a status, pair it with a word, the way you would anywhere else on the site.

## Where an icon earns a place

Use an icon when it helps someone scan a repeated pattern. A list of three features can take three marks if the marks are genuinely different and the labels are clear. A list of three features with three identical sparkles is noise. The labels were doing the work. Let them.

Navigation can take icons when the destinations are few and familiar, and when the label is still visible. Hiding the label to save space is how people land in the wrong place. On a phone, a bar with four unlabeled marks is a memory test. Keep the word. If the word does not fit, you have too many destinations, not a need for cleverer pictures.

Do not icon a heading that is already clear. A small drawing beside every section title adds a column of clutter and asks the reader to decode a metaphor they did not need. Save the system for controls and for the occasional list. A page of paragraphs usually wants zero icons. That is a successful use of the set.

Inside a product, icons carry more weight because people repeat the same actions. A marketing site is closer to a document. The ratio flips. Fewer marks, more sentences. If you are porting a product's icon set onto the marketing homepage, bring the ones that label real actions and leave the rest in the app.

## Names, targets, and the invisible label

The W3C organizes WCAG 2 under four principles: perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust. An icon used as a button sits in the middle of that. A person has to perceive it, operate it, and understand what it will do. WCAG 2.2 is the version W3C encourages. You do not meet that hope with a pretty SVG and a click handler on a div.

Give every icon control an accessible name. "Close," "Open menu," "Search." The visible label can be the name when it is on screen. When the label is visually hidden, the name still has to be in the markup. A title attribute that only appears on hover is a weak substitute, and it does nothing on a phone.

Make the target large enough to hit. A 16-pixel glyph with no padding is a miss on a phone and a miss for anyone with a tremor. The icon can stay visually small. The hit area should be closer to a fingertip. Alignment and padding are part of the grid decision, not a later CSS surprise.

Do not put the meaning in color alone, and do not convey it by animation alone. A bell that wiggles to mean "you have a notification" fails when motion is reduced and fails when the person cannot see the wiggle. A dot plus the word, or a count, survives. The icon set is not the place to be subtle about state.

## The download that breaks the set

Icon libraries are useful as a starting point and dangerous as a habit. The first person downloads a set that is close enough. The next person needs a calendar mark the set does not have, so they grab it from somewhere else. By the third page, the header is a group photo of strangers. The fix is a rule: new icons are drawn into the set, or the feature waits.

If you adopt an open set, adopt it whole and pin the version. Outline or solid, one size, the same stroke the set was designed with. Do not run the icons through a style filter that almost matches. Almost is the look you are trying to avoid. When the brand needs a custom mark for the product itself, commission that one mark and keep the interface icons plain. The logo can be special. The close button should not be.

Store the source in the repository, as SVG, named for the action. A React component per icon, or one sprite with an explicit list, keeps the stroke from being edited on a single page. Tailwind can set the size and the color at the point of use. It should not be asked to invent the drawing. When someone pastes a new path into a page file, the review should catch it the way it would catch a new font.

Figma, or Illustrator for the more drawn marks, is the right place to check the row. Line the icons up on the grid, in the color they will be on the site, at the size they will be in the header. Optical imbalances show up in a row that a single artboard will hide. A circle always looks lighter than a square at the same nominal weight. Adjust the drawing, then export again. Do not fix it with a one-off scale on the website.

## States, files, and the row in the header

Draw the states you actually use, and only those. Default, hover if you still support it, focus, and disabled. Focus must be visible on the control, not only a color shift inside a 16-pixel shape. Disabled should look quiet and must not be the only way a person learns that an action exists. If a state needs a tooltip to be understood, the label is missing.

Export once, from the grid, and commit the files. A designer who tweaks a single path in the browser will ship a stroke that no longer matches its neighbors. Review the header as a row at the size it ships: the marks should feel like one instrument, evenly padded, sitting on the same center line as the type. If one icon looks heavier, redraw that icon. Do not wrap it in a colored chip to hide the mismatch.

When a campaign asks for a special mark, give the campaign an illustration, not a new interface icon. The header returns to the quiet set the day the campaign ends. That separation is what keeps the system small enough to keep.

## How many is enough

Count the icons on the homepage. If you are past a dozen, ask which ones a visitor could lose without getting lost. Feature grids are the usual surplus. Three clear sentences will beat six vague sentences with medals pinned to them. Cut the icons first. If the sentence was only there to justify the icon, cut the sentence too.

A marketing site can ship with a very small set: menu, close, arrow, external link, and maybe search. Add more when a repeated pattern appears in the product or the docs. A set of forty, designed in a week because a brand project felt like it should include one, will be half unused and half misused. Unused icons become the place people grab from when they are in a hurry, which is how the wrong metaphor shows up next to a serious claim.

Document the metaphors you refused. A lightbulb for ideas, a rocket for launch, a handshake for partnership: these are the downloads that make every site look like the same site. If your offer is specific, your pictures of it should be specific too, and your icons should get out of the way. Quiet is a position.

Review the set when you review the type. They drift together. A new display face that is very sharp will make a rounded icon set look accidental, and the reverse is true too. You do not have to redraw the world. You do have to look at the header as one object.

If you want help settling a small system before it spreads across the site, book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). Bring the header and one page that feels busy. The decision is usually to remove, then to redraw what remains on a single grid.

Motion is the next place a quiet system gets loud. [Motion on a sales page](/blog/motion-on-a-sales-page) is the next piece, because an icon that bounces, and a page that will not sit still, ask the buyer to wait for an offer that should have been still and readable.
